title: A holy Father and a grain of wheat
source_text: Καινὸν οὖν γέγονεν, ἐξ οὗ πέπονθε χρόνου ὁ Ἰησοῦς, κἀκεῖνο, λέγω δὲ τὸ κατὰ τὴν πόλιν καὶ πᾶν τὸ κατὰ τὸ ἔθνος καὶ τὸ κατὰ τὴν ἀθρόαν γένεσιν ἔθνους Χριστιανῶν ὡσπερεὶ τεχθέντος εἰσάπαξ· καινὸν δὲ καὶ τὸ τοὺς ξένους „τῶν διαθηκῶν“ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ ἀλλοτρίους τῶν ἐπαγγελιῶν τοὺς μακρὰν τῆς ἀληθείας δυνάμει τινὶ θείᾳ παραδέχεσθαι αὐτήν. ταῦτα δὲ οὐκ ἀνθρώπου γόητος ἦν ἀλλ᾿ ἔργα θεοῦ, πέμψαντος τῶν αὑτοῦ ἀγγελμάτων ἕνεκα τὸν αὑτοῦ ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ λόγον, (οὕτως) ὠμῶς κολασθέντι, ὡς τὴν ὠμότητα κατηγορεῖσθαι τῶν ἀδίκως αὐτὸν κολασάντων, καὶ ἀνδρειότατα ὑπομείναντα καὶ μετὰ πάσης. πρᾳότητος· οὐ διέφθειρε δὲ ἡ κόλασις αὐτοῦ τὰ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀγγέλματα ἀλλ᾿, εἰ δεῖ ουτως ὀνομάσαι, εἰς γνῶσιν αὐτὰ ἤγαγεν· ὡς καὶ αὐτὸς ἐδίδαξεν ὁ Ἰησοῦς λέγων· „ἐὰν μὴ ὁ κόκκος τοῦ σίτου πεσὼν εἰς τὴν γῆν ἀποθάνῃ, αὐτὸς μόνος μένει· ἐὰν δὲ ἀποθάνῃ, πολὺν καρπὸν φέρει.“ ἀποθανὼν οὖν „ὁ κόκκος τοῦ σίτου“ Ἰησοῦς „πολὺν καρπὸν“ ἤνεγκε, καὶ ἀεὶ ὁ πατὴρ προνοεῖ τῶν ἐκ τοῦ θανάτου τοῦ κόκκου „τοῦ σίτου“ γεγενημένων καὶ γινομένων ἔτι καὶ ἐσομένων καρπῶν. ὅσιος οὖν πατὴρ ὁ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πατὴρ, „τοῦ ἰδίου“ μὴ φεισάμενος „υἱοῦ“ „ἀλλ᾿ ὑπὲρ ἡμῶν πάντων“ παραδοὺς „αὐτὸν“ ἀμνὸν ὄντα ἑαυτοῦ. ἵν᾿ ἄρῃ „τὴν ἁμαρτίαν τοῦ κόσμου“ ὁ ὑπὲρ παντὸς αὐτοῦ ἀποθνῄσκων „ἀμνὸς θεοῦ“· δι᾿ ὃν οὐκ ἀναγκαζόμενος ἀλλ᾿ ἑκὼν ὑπέμεινε τὰ ἀπὸ τῶν ὑβριστῶν αὐτῷ προσαγόμενα. εἶτα μετὰ ταῦτα ὁ Κέλσος, ἐπαναλαμβάνων τὸν πρὸς τοὺς βλασφημοῦντας τὰ ἀγάλματα λόγον, φησίν· οἵδε δὲ, οὓς σὺ βλασφημεῖς, ἐνῆν μὲν εἰπεῖν ὅτι καὶ αὐτοὶ βούλονται (καὶ) διὰ τοῦτ᾿ ἀνέχονται βλασφημούμενοι· τὰ γὰρ ἴσα τοῖς ἴσοις παραβαλεῖν κράτιστον· ἀλλ᾿ οὗτοί γε καὶ σφόδρα ἀμύνονται τὸν βλασφημοῦντα, ἤτοι γε φεύγοντα διὰ τοῦτο καὶ κρυπτόμενον ἢ ἁλισκόμενον καὶ ἀπολλύμενον. οὐ βλασφημοῦντας ουν ἀλλ᾿ ἀπελαύνοντας ἀπὸ τῶν ξοάνων καὶ τῶν ἀνθρωπίνων σωμάτων καὶ ψυχῶν Χριστιανοὺς ἀμύνεσθαι νομίζουσιν οἱ δαίμονες. μὴ νοῶν γὰρ τὸ γινόμενον ἀλη θές τι κατὰ τὸν τόπον ὁ Κέλσος εἴρηκεν· ἀληθὲς γὰρ τὸ φαύλων δαιμόνων πληρουμένας τὰς τῶν καταδικαζόντων Χριστιανοὺς ψυχὰς καὶ τῶν προδιδόντων καὶ τῶν εὐδοκούντων Χριστιανοῖς προσπολεμεῖν.
pass_a_gloss: New (καινόν) therefore has happened, from the time Jesus suffered, that too: I mean the matter of the city and all regarding the nation (ἔθνος) and the sudden (ἀθρόαν) birth (γένεσιν) of a nation of Christians as though born (τεχθέντος) once for all (εἰσάπαξ); new also that strangers (ξένους) to the covenants (διαθηκῶν) of God and aliens (ἀλλοτρίους) from the promises (ἐπαγγελιῶν), those far (μακράν) from the truth, by a certain divine power received (παραδέχεσθαι) it. These were not of a sorcerer man (ἀνθρώπου γόητος) but works (ἔργα) of God, who sent for the sake of his own messages (ἀγγελμάτων) his own Word in Jesus (τὸν αὑτοῦ ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ λόγον), [Jesus] so cruelly (ὠμῶς) punished that the cruelty (ὠμότητα) is accused against (κατηγορεῖσθαι) those who unjustly (ἀδίκως) punished him, and [the Word] most courageously (ἀνδρειότατα) enduring (ὑπομείναντα) and with all gentleness (πρᾳότητος). His punishment did not destroy (διέφθειρε) the messages of God but, if one must so name it, led (ἤγαγεν) them into knowledge (γνῶσιν); as Jesus himself taught saying: unless the grain (κόκκος) of wheat (σίτου) falling into the earth dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (καρπόν). So having died, the grain of wheat Jesus bore much fruit, and always the Father provides for (προνοεῖ) the fruits that have come about, are still coming about and will be from the death of the grain of wheat. Holy (ὅσιος) therefore a father is the Father of Jesus, not sparing (φεισάμενος) his own Son but handing him over (παραδούς) for us all, being his own lamb (ἀμνόν), so that the Lamb of God dying for all of it (ὑπὲρ παντὸς αὐτοῦ, i.e. the world) might take away (ἄρῃ) the sin of the world; on account of which (δι᾿ ὅν) not compelled (οὐκ ἀναγκαζόμενος) but willingly (ἑκών) he endured the things brought upon him by the insolent (ὑβριστῶν). Then after these Celsus, resuming (ἐπαναλαμβάνων) the argument against those who blaspheme the statues, says: [quotation as in 41]. Not as blaspheming therefore but as driving away (ἀπελαύνοντας) from the wooden images (ξοάνων) and human bodies and souls do the demons think (νομίζουσιν) they avenge themselves on Christians. For not understanding (μὴ νοῶν) what happens Celsus has said something true on this point (κατὰ τὸν τόπον): for it is true that the souls of those condemning (καταδικαζόντων) Christians and of those betraying (προδιδόντων) and of those pleased (εὐδοκούντων) to make war upon (προσπολεμεῖν) Christians are filled (πληρουμένας) with base demons (φαύλων δαιμόνων).

lemmas.lemma: τὸν αὑτοῦ ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ λόγον

pass_b_english: So something new has indeed happened since the time when Jesus suffered: I mean what befell the city and the whole nation, and the sudden birth of a nation of Christians, born, as it were, all at once (Isaiah 66:8). New too is this, that those who were strangers to “the covenants” of God and aliens from the promises (Ephesians 2:12), those far from the truth, have received it by a certain divine power. These were not the doings of a human sorcerer but the works of God. He sent, for the sake of his messages, his own Word in Jesus, who was punished so cruelly that the cruelty is charged against those who punished him unjustly, and who bore it with the greatest courage and with all gentleness.

His punishment did not destroy God’s messages but, if it must be put this way, made them known; as Jesus himself taught when he said, “Unless the grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). So by dying, Jesus, “the grain of wheat,” bore “much fruit,” and the Father always takes care of the fruits that have come, still come, and will yet come from the death of the grain “of wheat.” A holy father, then, is the Father of Jesus, who did not spare “his own Son but gave him up for us all” (Romans 8:32), him who was his own lamb, so that “the Lamb of God,” who dies for the whole world, might take away “the sin of the world” (John 1:29). And for the world’s sake he endured, not under compulsion but willingly, the things the insolent inflicted on him.

Then, after this, Celsus takes up again his argument against those who blaspheme the statues, and says: “But as for these whom you blaspheme, one could have said that they too wish it, and for that reason bear being blasphemed; for it is best to compare like with like. But these at least take vigorous vengeance on the one who blasphemes them, so that he either flees for this reason and hides, or is caught and perishes.” It is not, then, as blasphemers that the demons think they take vengeance on Christians, but as those who drive them out of the images and out of human bodies and souls. For without understanding what happens, Celsus has said something true on this point. It is true that the souls of those who condemn Christians, of those who betray them, and of those who delight in making war on Christians, are filled with wicked demons.

choices.choice: Origen answers Celsus’s questions in 41 point by point: ‘What new thing has happened?’ (καινόν), ‘not a human sorcerer’ (ἀνθρώπου γόητος), ‘sent ... for the sake of messages ... punished so cruelly’ (ἀγγελμάτων ἕνεκα, ὠμῶς κολασθέντι), ‘destroyed the messages’ (διέφθειρε), and ‘What father is so unholy?’ answered by ‘Holy, then (ὅσιος), is the Father’. The English keeps the same words in both places. ‘A nation born all at once’ (ἔθνους ... τεχθέντος εἰσάπαξ) alludes to LXX Isaiah 66:8 (εἰ ἐγεννήθη ἔθνος εἰς ἅπαξ); cited. ‘Strangers to the covenants ... aliens’ echoes Ephesians 2:12 (ξένοι τῶν διαθηκῶν τῆς ἐπαγγελίας); ‘far’ (μακράν) echoes Ephesians 2:13 and 2:17; only 2:12 cited inline. In τὸν αὑτοῦ ἐν τῷ Ἰησοῦ λόγον ... κολασθέντι ... ὑπομείναντα, the dative ‘punished’ goes with Jesus and the accusative ‘enduring’ goes with the Word; English keeps one subject (‘his own Word in Jesus, who was punished ... and who bore it’), which matches Origen’s point that the Word in Jesus endured. The (οὕτως) supplied by the editor is followed. ‘If it must be put this way’ renders εἰ δεῖ οὕτως ὀνομάσαι. ὑπὲρ παντὸς αὐτοῦ: αὐτοῦ refers back to τοῦ κόσμου, so ‘for the whole world’; δι᾿ ὅν is taken the same way (‘for its sake’). ‘Dies for all’ may also echo Hebrews 2:9 (ὑπὲρ παντὸς γεύσηται θανάτου); not cited. ‘Lamb’ in ‘his own lamb’ is lower case (a description); ‘the Lamb of God’ is capitalised as a title of Christ. ‘The Father always takes care of the fruits’ and ‘not under compulsion but willingly’ are Origen’s own wording, not quotations. ὅσιος οὖν πατὴρ ὁ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πατήρ is rendered ‘A holy father, then, is the Father of Jesus’, keeping the word ‘father’ so the answer to ‘What father is so unholy?’ is exact.
εἰς γνῶσιν αὐτὰ ἤγαγεν: 'brought them to men’s knowledge' ('men's' added) changed to 'made them known'
ὅσιος οὖν πατὴρ ὁ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ πατήρ: 'Holy, then, is the Father' changed to 'A holy father, then, is the Father', to answer Celsus's 'What father is so unholy?' word for word
ἀμνὸν ὄντα ἑαυτοῦ: 'since he was his own lamb' (added 'since') changed to 'him who was his own lamb'
δι᾿ ὅν: 'for its sake' (could be misread as the sin) changed to 'for the world’s sake'
Scripture checked: Isaiah 66:8 LXX (ἐτέχθη ἔθνος εἰς ἅπαξ), Ephesians 2:12, John 12:24, Romans 8:32, John 1:29 all match; Celsus quotation identical to 41
